title: Can People Really Get Hysterical Strength?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss hysterical strength, the reported ability of people in extreme emergencies to lift or move objects far heavier than they normally could. They recount a Texas case in which a grandmother, nicknamed Bootsy, lifted a running riding lawnmower off her granddaughter Evie, who had jumped in front of it and lost four toes. They note medical science does not recognize hysterical strength because it cannot be replicated in a study. They link it to the fight or flight response: adrenaline, increased heart rate and respiration, and skeletal muscle contraction driven by electrical impulses from the brain. They also explain why the body cannot stay in that state permanently, since homeostasis is the goal and prolonged hyper-arousal wears down the heart and weakens immunity. The episode opens and closes with ad reads for the Camry.
topics: electrical impulses from brain to muscles

segments.title: Hysterical strength and lack of medical recognition
segments.summary: The hosts define hysterical strength and note medical science does not recognize it, since it cannot be replicated in a controlled study. Cases are well documented through witnesses.

segments.title: Fight or flight response and muscle power
segments.summary: Explanation of the fight or flight response: sympathetic activation, adrenaline release, faster heart rate and respiration, and muscles contracting from electrical impulses from the brain. The hosts discuss how the surge lets people tap untapped muscular strength.
